name: yaze-ag
why: A Z80 emulator lets you run and step through old 8-bit machine code and CP/M software.

brief.what_it_is: YAZE-AG (Yet Another Z80 Emulator by AG) is a Z80 CPU emulator, written by Andreas Gerlich, that runs inside a host UNIX, Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Cygwin or Raspberry Pi system. It is a CPU emulator, not a CP/M emulator: it runs an original CP/M or a replacement such as the CP/M 3.1 replacement ZPM3N10 or the CP/M 2.2 replacement Superdos. Its inputs are the emulated machine's boot files and disk images (.ydsk files, up to 64 MB), plus host directories that can be mounted as CP/M drives. Its output is the emulated CP/M session on the terminal, with serial-line access to real PC serial ports.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to provide an exact simulation of the Z80 microprocessor so that old 8-bit software can run. The homepage says it is 'designed to provide an exact simulation of the Z80 microprocessor', and it grew out of yaze-1.10 with added CP/M 3.1 support.
brief.how_it_works: The emulator is a Z80 core with an emulated Memory Management Unit (MMU), which the author developed from Michael Haardt's page-table idea. A BIOS (ybios.c and BIOS3 *.Z80 files) provides CP/M 3.1 features such as date, disk-change, xmove and multi-I/O. Disk images are .ydsk files managed with the cdm utility, and the import/export utilities R.COM and W.COM move files between the host and the emulated system.

commands_seen.context: Typed at the emulated CP/M prompt; creates CPM3.COM so CP/M 3.1 can be restarted under CP/M 3.1 or 2.2.
BOOTSYS usage: makes BOOTSYS search drive P: for CPM3.SYS, load and relocate it, and start CP/M 3.1.
Monitor command that sets the emulator to maximum speed.
Monitor command that limits the emulator to 4000 kHz (4.0 MHz), for running games written for that clock rate.
Command the author suggests running in the emulator as a tip for getting help.

brief.install_notes: On UNIX/Linux/Cygwin/macOS/Raspberry Pi you build from the yaze-ag-2.51.3.tar.gz source, using Makefiles for the listed platforms. The author says to edit the Makefile, and the INSTALL-2.51.3 file (not fetched) explains the process. You start the emulator with the shell script 'yaze' (which drives the binary 'yaze_bin'), and yaze(1) describes what it installs on first run. Windows users can use the standalone binaries built with Cygwin, or the yaze.bat batch file, or a desktop link. Verify downloads with the SHA256SUMS file and the author's GPG key. Hardware listed includes Raspberry Pi 1, 2, 3, 4, Banana Pi M3, Orange Pi Plus2 and Radxa Rock boards, plus Solaris on SPARC and x86_64. No accounts are needed.
brief.standout: It emulates undocumented Z80 opcodes and includes a configurable clock speed, so software written for 4, 8 or 12 MHz machines can run at its original speed. It also ships BOOTSYS, a loader that restarts CP/M 3.1 from inside CP/M and gets around the failure of the older CPMLDR and ZPM3LDR loaders with the 43 KB CPM3.SYS.
brief.status: quiet. The homepage calls 2.51.3 the 'final release' (2022-02-16), and the page's last change is dated February 16, 2022. I saw no later release or commit, so there is no sign of active work after that date.
brief.caveats: It is a Z80 CPU emulator, not a turnkey CP/M machine: you need a CP/M boot file (yaze-cpm3.boot or yaze.boot) and disk images. Building from source means editing the Makefile by hand. The author says serial lines were not tested on a Mac, and the Windows version runs under Cygwin. The author's English is self-described as 'not that good'. The homepage says the author is no longer adding features but there are no known bugs. I did not see an explicit software license for yaze-ag itself on the pages I read, only that ZSM4, the bundled assembler, is GPLv2.
quotes: YAZE-AG is a Z80-CPU-Emulator and NOT a CP/M-Emulator!
It is fast, emulates undocumented opcodes, and passes instruction regression tests against real Z80 hardware.
I believe this version runs quite stable.
fetch_log: https://agl.yaze-ag.de/ (homepage): fetched OK, about 40 KB of text. It serves as the README-equivalent page and links to INSTALL-2.51.3, yaze(1), yaze-ag.doc and README-2.51.3, but those URLs were not given in full on the page, so I did not follow them. Five-fetch budget left unused.

judge.reason: It offers a hands-on CP/M sandbox backed by a Z80 emulator that handles undocumented opcodes and configurable clock speeds, making an old computing platform tangible.

entry.title: yaze-ag
entry.tldr: A Z80 CPU emulator that boots real CP/M 2.2 and 3.1 in your terminal, with undocumented opcodes and adjustable clock speed.
entry.deeper_look:
YAZE-AG (Yet Another Z80 Emulator, by Andreas Gerlich) emulates the Z80, the 8-bit processor behind a generation of home computers and CP/M business machines. It grew out of yaze-1.10 and adds CP/M 3.1 support. The homepage says it is "designed to provide an exact simulation of the Z80 microprocessor".

The author's first line is blunt: "YAZE-AG is a Z80-CPU-Emulator and NOT a CP/M-Emulator!" You supply an operating system, either original CP/M or a replacement such as ZPM3N10 or Superdos, plus disk images in the .ydsk format. The `cdm` utility manages those images. Host directories can be mounted as CP/M drives, and the R.COM and W.COM utilities move files between the host and the emulated machine.

Under the hood is a Z80 core with an emulated memory management unit, built from Michael Haardt's page-table idea. A custom BIOS provides CP/M 3.1 features such as date, disk change and multi-I/O. The emulator also handles undocumented opcodes and can be throttled to a chosen clock speed, so software written for a 4 MHz machine runs at the speed its authors expected.

The door it opens is old 8-bit computing: a whole operating system, its tools and its software, small enough to understand, running on a CPU whose every instruction you can study.
entry.install:
brew install yaze-ag
# You also need a CP/M boot file (yaze-cpm3.boot or yaze.boot) and disk images. Start with the `yaze` script, which drives `yaze_bin`. No accounts or extra hardware needed.

try_this.what_happens: Starts the emulator through its wrapper script, which drives yaze_bin, and boots into the emulated CP/M session.
At the emulator's monitor, limits the CPU to 4.0 MHz so games written for that clock run at their original speed.
Removes the speed limit and runs the emulated Z80 flat out.

entry.whats_unique: It emulates undocumented Z80 opcodes and lets you set the clock speed to match original hardware. It also ships BOOTSYS, which restarts CP/M 3.1 from inside CP/M.
entry.caveats: The author calls 2.51.3 (February 2022) the final release and is adding no more features, and it is a bare CPU emulator that needs a CP/M boot file and disk images supplied by you.
